title: Quantum many-body framework for passive-scalar turbulence
authors: Zhaoyuan Meng, Long Wang, Guowei He
abstract: How spatial structures manifest in multi-time correlations is a fundamental question in turbulence. We develop a non-Hermitian bosonic framework that unifies equal-time anomalous statistics and their temporal propagation within a common operator representation. A continuous Wegner flow reorganizes stochastic mode couplings in an extended wave-frequency space. Applied to the Taylor-Kraichnan model, the framework recovers the established equal-time hierarchy and constructs multi-time contributions through propagators acting on successively smaller sets of active fields. This construction separates uniform transport from intrinsic relative dynamics and shows how a higher-order equal-time state evolves under a generator acting only on the fields that remain dynamically active. Within an isotropic radial closure, we derive an explicit fourth-order two-time zero mode scaling function that describe how relative dispersion progressively weakens sensitivity to the initial separation. The framework thus connects spatial intermittency to temporal evolution by identifying how the sequence of observation times determines the propagation of equal-time anomalous structures.
summary: This work develops a sophisticated non-Hermitian bosonic framework to unify the description of equal-time and multi-time anomalous statistics in passive-scalar turbulence. By applying a continuous Wegner flow, the authors simplify the governing stochastic equation, leading to the analytical derivation of a scaling function that precisely describes how spatial correlations decay over time lags.
main_problem: The paper addresses the fundamental challenge of connecting the spatial organization of fluctuations to their temporal evolution in turbulent systems, specifically focusing on the propagation of equal-time anomalous statistics across multiple observation times.
main_result: The authors derive an explicit fourth-order two-time zero mode scaling function, $\Phi_{2,2}(s)$, which analytically describes how relative dispersion weakens sensitivity to the initial separation in passive-scalar turbulence.
method: A non-Hermitian bosonic framework is developed, utilizing second quantization and a continuous Wegner flow to map the stochastic partial differential equation onto a solvable, diagonal effective Hamiltonian.
model_or_system: The study is applied to passive-scalar turbulence, modeled using the Taylor-Kraichnan (TK) equation. The theoretical machinery involves lifting the stochastic PDE to an extended wave-frequency space and analyzing the resulting bosonic Hamiltonian.
key_observables: Equal-time anomalous statistics, multi-time Eulerian correlation functions ($C_E^n$), and the relative zero-mode scaling function $\Phi_{2,2}(s)$.
important_parameters: The analysis considers the inertial range, time lags ($	au$), and spatial separations ($r$), leading to scaling exponents like $\zeta_4$.
main_assumptions: The derivation relies on an isotropic radial closure and the ability to separate the dynamics into diagonal (uniform advection/diffusion) and off-diagonal (stochastic coupling) parts.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates the entire theoretical pipeline: from the original PDE to second quantization, lifting to extended space, applying the Wegner flow, and finally reconstructing the statistics.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the non-Hermitian bosonic framework via the Wegner flow to simplify the stochastic PDE. It then analyzes the equal-time sector (recovering the Kraichnan hierarchy) before tackling the multi-time sector, culminating in the derivation and solution of the scaling function $\Phi_{2,2}(s)$ for the two-time correlation.
why_interesting: While focused on fluid dynamics, the use of a non-Hermitian bosonic framework and the mapping of stochastic PDEs to solvable quantum Hamiltonians provides powerful, generalizable mathematical tools applicable to open quantum systems and quantum field theory in non-equilibrium settings.
